labs.title: IPv4: verify the provided plan and forwarding path
labs.bridge: Foundation for client LANs behind JNN/CPN; this is not their approved addressing plan.
labs.objective: Compare the assigned address, prefix and gateway with the provided plan, then interpret next-hop forwarding. Subnet calculation is not required.
labs.scenario: A fictional client can reach its gateway but cannot reach a server in a different /24. The test bench has no proxy ARP, VPN or more-specific route.
concepts: An IPv4 prefix separates network bits from host bits. /24 is 255.255.255.0; /16 is 255.255.0.0.
With /16, 10.20.30.50 and 10.20.40.20 appear on the same 10.20.0.0 network. With /24, they are on different networks.

On Ethernet, Address Resolution Protocol (ARP) resolves an IPv4 next hop to a MAC address. Local delivery resolves the destination; remote delivery resolves the gateway. The most-specific matching route wins, so /16 on-link overrides /0.
labs.baseline:
Approved client: 10.20.30.50/24
Gateway: 10.20.30.1
Remote service: 10.20.40.20:443
Client LAN: 10.20.30.0/24
Server LAN: 10.20.40.0/24
labs.observed:
Client: 10.20.30.50/16
Gateway: 10.20.30.1
Connected route: 10.20.0.0/16 on-link
Default route: 0.0.0.0/0 via 10.20.30.1

evidence.title: Read the address and prefix
evidence.output:
IPAddress: 10.20.30.50
PrefixLength: 16
AddressState: Preferred
evidence.meaning: The address is usable, but the prefix differs from the /24 baseline.

evidence.title: Compare gateway and destination tests
evidence.output:
Gateway ICMP test (separate supplied observation): success
RemoteAddress: 10.20.40.20
RemotePort: 443
TcpTestSucceeded: False
evidence.meaning: A reachable gateway does not mean the host is actually choosing it for this destination.

evidence.title: Inspect the packet-path observation
evidence.command: Supplied packet observation; no command is executed
evidence.output:
Client broadcasts: Who has 10.20.40.20?
No ARP reply. No destination TCP packet reaches router.
evidence.meaning: The workstation is trying local delivery to the remote server. This narrows the fault before transport or DNS is blamed.

decisions.question: Which finding explains all three observations?

options.label: The remote DNS record is missing.
options.feedback: The test uses an IP address; DNS does not explain the on-link ARP attempt.

options.label: The /16 prefix makes the remote /24 appear local.
options.feedback: The connected /16 route wins over /0, so the host ARPs for the destination rather than forwarding through the gateway.

options.label: The satellite terminal must be reacquired.
options.feedback: The failure occurs in local next-hop selection before the router receives the service traffic.

decisions.question: Which correction belongs in the approved change?

options.label: Restore the client prefix to /24 and keep the documented address and gateway.
options.feedback: This restores the intended subnet boundary. Record the prior value and a rollback plan before an authorized change.

options.label: Add an arbitrary static route for every failed server.
options.feedback: That hides the incorrect baseline and grows fragile exceptions.

options.label: Disable the host firewall.
options.feedback: Firewall removal does not correct the on-link route selection.

decisions.question: Which recovery evidence is sufficient for this client task?

options.label: The gateway responds to one ping.
options.feedback: This was already true during the fault; it does not prove remote service delivery.

options.label: The IP address still begins with 10.20.
options.feedback: Shared leading octets do not establish the correct prefix or user outcome.

options.label: Confirm /24, gateway forwarding, TCP service access and the receiving-user exchange.
options.feedback: These checks tie the corrected configuration to the original failed task without inferring other hosts are fixed.

labs.recovery:
PrefixLength: 24
Remote packet next hop: 10.20.30.1
TcpTestSucceeded to 10.20.40.20:443: True
Fictional receiving user confirms new test report R-104.
labs.impact: Leader brief: one client had an incorrect subnet boundary, preventing remote delivery before the node transport. R-104 was received after the approved correction; other clients remain outside this test.
labs.practical: Use the instructor-provided addressing plan in an isolated client/router lab. Compare Get-NetIPAddress and the supplied route/neighbor evidence with that plan. Identify a changed prefix, explain its effect on the packet path, restore the documented setting through the approved lab procedure and verify the receiving-user task. No subnet calculation is assessed.

labs.title: VLANs: link up does not mean the right LAN
labs.bridge: Useful at access switches and server virtual networks supporting mission nodes; port numbers and VLANs are fictional.
labs.objective: Trace an untagged access frame into its VLAN and check the uplink before changing a host.
labs.scenario: A client in the intended staff VLAN cannot resolve its local gateway. The physical link is up.
concepts: A virtual LAN (VLAN) separates Layer 2 traffic. An access port places ordinary untagged client frames into its access VLAN; an 802.1Q trunk can carry multiple VLANs.
A VLAN is a Layer 2 broadcast domain. The host IP alone cannot place the cable into the correct VLAN.
Check operational switchport mode, access VLAN, VLAN existence and trunk forwarding. An allowed list alone does not establish spanning-tree forwarding.
labs.baseline:
Client: 10.20.30.50/24; gateway 10.20.30.1
Access port Gi1/0/7: VLAN 30
Uplink Gi1/0/48: trunk, VLAN 30 allowed and forwarding
labs.observed:
interface GigabitEthernet1/0/7
 switchport mode access
 switchport access vlan 20
! Gi1/0/48 carries VLANs 20,30

evidence.title: Inspect the client port
evidence.output:
Operational Mode: static access
Access Mode VLAN: 20 (TRAINING-OTHER)
evidence.meaning: An active link can still put the client in the wrong broadcast domain.

evidence.title: Inspect VLAN and trunk forwarding
evidence.output:
Gi1/0/48: trunking
Vlans allowed: 20,30
Vlans allowed and active: 20,30
Vlans in spanning tree forwarding state and not pruned: 20,30
evidence.meaning: The supplied uplink can carry the intended VLAN; this rules out one alternative cause.

evidence.title: Check host and gateway placement
evidence.output:
Client MAC is learned on Gi1/0/7 in VLAN 20.
Gateway 10.20.30.1 is on VLAN 30.
Client address/prefix match the approved /24.
evidence.meaning: The client and its gateway are separated at Layer 2 despite compatible IP settings.

decisions.question: What is the supported fault?

options.label: The client access port is assigned to VLAN 20 instead of VLAN 30.
options.feedback: The MAC placement and switchport evidence locate the mismatch; the trunk already forwards VLAN 30.

options.label: A DNS timeout caused the VLAN change.
options.feedback: ARP to a gateway uses its IP; DNS does not assign switch access VLANs.

options.label: The router needs a new default route.
options.feedback: The workstation cannot yet reach its own gateway at Layer 2.

decisions.question: Which lab change corrects the documented mismatch?

options.label: Allow every VLAN on every trunk.
options.feedback: The uplink already forwards VLAN 30. Expanding access changes isolation without addressing this port.

options.label: Move the client to an unrecorded IP range.
options.feedback: That abandons the approved design instead of correcting the wrong access membership.

options.label: On the authorized lab port, replace switchport access vlan 20 with switchport access vlan 30.
options.feedback: Use the confirmed physical port, device syntax and approved VLAN. Preserve segmentation and rollback information.

decisions.question: What establishes recovery?

options.label: The link LED is green.
options.feedback: Link was up during the fault.

options.label: Confirm access VLAN 30, correct MAC learning, gateway ARP and the remote staff transaction.
options.feedback: Layer 2 placement and the user task are separate acceptance checks.

options.label: The trunk allows VLAN 30.
options.feedback: This also was true before the correction; the client port still needed fixing.

labs.recovery:
Gi1/0/7: static access, VLAN 30
Client MAC learned in VLAN 30
Gateway ARP resolved
Receiving-user test report R-105 accepted.
labs.impact: Leader brief: one access port placed a workstation in the wrong LAN. Corrected membership restored the tested user exchange; no trunk or wider segmentation change was needed.
labs.practical: Use an isolated switch or supported emulator. Label two access VLANs and a trunk, inspect membership at each hop, then change only the assigned training port. Explain why physical link status was insufficient.

labs.title: DNS: separate name failure from TCP reachability
labs.bridge: Supports mission applications on node-hosted infrastructure; resolver values are not an Army baseline.
labs.objective: Compare answers from the configured and designated resolver, then separate DNS, TCP, TLS and user acceptance.
labs.scenario: The application hostname fails, but the remote IP accepts TCP connections. The fictional app uses a single A record and no load balancer.
concepts: DNS maps a name to records; TCP tests a specific address and port. These are different dependencies.
NXDOMAIN is a negative DNS answer, not the same as a query timeout. Compare the exact query and server before changing a record.
A TCP 443 success does not prove a valid TLS certificate, authentication or current application data. Keep the hostname for normal application verification.
labs.baseline:
Client resolver: 10.20.30.10
report.training.example A 10.20.40.20
Application TCP port: 443
labs.observed:
Configured client resolver: 10.20.30.99
Approved resolver: 10.20.30.10
Client IP/prefix/gateway: match baseline

evidence.title: Test the known service IP
evidence.output:
RemoteAddress: 10.20.40.20
RemotePort: 443
TcpTestSucceeded: True
evidence.meaning: This establishes TCP connectivity to one endpoint, not the entire application.

evidence.title: Query the configured resolver
evidence.output:
DNS response summary: NXDOMAIN
Server: 10.20.30.99
evidence.meaning: The configured resolver answers negatively for the exact fictional name.

evidence.title: Compare the approved resolver
evidence.output:
Name: report.training.example
Type: A
IPAddress: 10.20.40.20
evidence.meaning: The supplied comparison supports a client resolver mismatch. It does not establish every DNS server or record is healthy.

decisions.question: Which fault is supported by these results?

options.label: TCP 443 is blocked across the entire network.
options.feedback: The explicit TCP test succeeded to the selected server IP.

options.label: The application certificate is definitely valid.
options.feedback: No TLS handshake or certificate validation is shown.

options.label: The client uses a resolver that lacks the required answer.
options.feedback: The two explicit queries isolate a resolver-dependent difference alongside working TCP reachability.

decisions.question: What is the appropriate correction for this baseline?

options.label: Use a permanent hosts-file entry and ignore DNS.
options.feedback: That creates a separate mapping and hides the assigned resolver error.

options.label: Restore the approved resolver assignment through the authorized static or DHCP management path.
options.feedback: Correct the configuration owner, confirm the effective value, and re-query. Do not send private queries to an arbitrary public resolver.

options.label: Browse by IP and bypass certificate warnings.
options.feedback: That can break hostname validation and authentication; it does not restore the intended service path.

decisions.question: Which evidence supports the user-facing recovery claim?

options.label: The default client resolver now returns the expected A record, TCP works, TLS validates and a new report is received.
options.feedback: Each dependency is checked separately, ending with the receiving user.

options.label: The IP still responds on port 443.
options.feedback: This was true during the fault and does not verify resolution.

options.label: A cached page opens on the client.
options.feedback: A cached page can open with no current server exchange.

labs.recovery:
Default resolver: 10.20.30.10
report.training.example A: 10.20.40.20
TCP 443: success; hostname certificate validation: success
New report R-106 acknowledged by receiving user.
labs.impact: Leader brief: the tested client had a name-resolution configuration fault while the server IP path remained usable. Named access and a fresh report exchange were verified after correction.
labs.practical: In an isolated lab, query a supplied fictional zone through two designated test resolvers. Record the query, answering server, response code and address. Verify TCP separately and explain why port 443 is not an application-health test.

labs.title: OSPF: interpret EXSTART and a missing route
labs.bridge: Routing foundation relevant to routed mission networks; no JNN/CPN router image or configuration template is assumed.
labs.objective: Use neighbor state, interface MTUs and route evidence to isolate an adjacency fault.
labs.scenario: Two training routers share a point-to-point OSPF link. Hellos are received, but the remote LAN is not learned. Neither router has an alternate route for it.
concepts: Open Shortest Path First (OSPF) exchanges Hellos and synchronizes link-state information before computing routes. EXSTART starts database description negotiation; FULL means database synchronization with that neighbor is complete.
An interface maximum transmission unit (MTU) mismatch can stop database description exchange. EXSTART alone is insufficient: compare both ends and other adjacency parameters.
A neighbor state and a route-table entry answer different questions. After FULL, confirm the expected destination prefix and then data-plane delivery.
labs.baseline:
Link: 10.255.0.0/30, area 0, point-to-point
R1: 10.255.0.1; R2: 10.255.0.2
Approved end-to-end link MTU: 1500
Expected remote LAN: 10.20.40.0/24
labs.observed:
R1 interface: MTU 1500, area 0, Hello 10, Dead 40
R2 interface: MTU 1400, area 0, Hello 10, Dead 40
Router IDs unique; authentication agrees in supplied lab inventory

evidence.title: Read adjacency state
evidence.output:
R1 neighbor 2.2.2.2: EXSTART/-
Address: 10.255.0.2
Interface: GigabitEthernet0/1
evidence.meaning: Hellos reached the peer, but database synchronization has not completed.

evidence.title: Compare both interface profiles
evidence.output:
R1: area 0, point-to-point, Hello 10, Dead 40
R2: area 0, point-to-point, Hello 10, Dead 40
Companion interface inventory: R1 MTU 1500; R2 MTU 1400
evidence.meaning: OSPF interface output and the supplied physical-interface MTU inventory must be read together. Actual display fields vary by release.

evidence.title: Look for the destination prefix
evidence.output:
No matching route or default route in the supplied R1 table.
Expected learned prefix: 10.20.40.0/24
evidence.meaning: A working adjacent link is not enough to forward toward the remote LAN.

decisions.question: Which hypothesis has the strongest supporting evidence?

options.label: Different OSPF process numbers necessarily prevent neighbors.
options.feedback: Process IDs are locally significant; the supplied MTU mismatch is a stronger finding.

options.label: The interface MTU mismatch is preventing successful database exchange.
options.feedback: The mismatch plus EXSTART supports this fault in the supplied case. Other EXSTART causes remain possible on real systems.

options.label: EXSTART means the remote LAN is fully reachable.
options.feedback: Neither adjacency synchronization nor a destination route is established.

decisions.question: Which authorized correction should be evaluated?

options.label: Align both interface MTUs with the validated 1500-byte lab path, then recheck adjacency and routes.
options.feedback: Use the documented link capability. Do not force a larger MTU on a path that cannot carry it.

options.label: Use mtu-ignore as the first fix without checking packet size.
options.feedback: Suppressing a check can hide a data-plane size problem; it is not a substitute for validating the path.

options.label: Restart every router in the exercise.
options.feedback: This adds disruption and does not correct the mismatched settings.

decisions.question: Which reference results support restored routing?

options.label: One Hello packet arrives.
options.feedback: Hellos were already reaching the peer.

options.label: The OSPF process exists.
options.feedback: A running process does not prove adjacency, a selected route or forwarding.

options.label: FULL adjacency, expected /24 via the peer, packet delivery and receiving-user confirmation.
options.feedback: This checks control plane, selected route, data plane and the staff task independently.

labs.recovery:
R1/R2 MTU: 1500 on validated path
Neighbor: FULL/-
O 10.20.40.0/24 [110/2] via 10.255.0.2
New report R-107 delivered and acknowledged.
labs.impact: Leader brief: the routers exchanged Hellos but did not complete routing synchronization. Correcting the documented MTU mismatch restored the tested route and report exchange; this does not prove all routes or packet sizes.
labs.practical: On an isolated two-router emulator, compare network type, area, timers, router IDs, authentication agreement and MTU. Observe EXSTART, FULL and the route table. Add a second fault later so the state name cannot become a memorized answer.

labs.title: DMVPN: underlay reachability is not an overlay
labs.bridge: Teaches underlay/overlay reasoning; no Army encryption or COMSEC setup is included.
labs.objective: Read tunnel-to-NBMA mappings and distinguish physical transport from NHRP and protected user traffic.
labs.scenario: A fictional spoke reaches the approved hub underlay IP but has no usable hub overlay session. Only the mapping excerpt is under investigation.
concepts: The underlay carries outer packets. Tunnel addresses identify the overlay; NBMA addresses identify transport endpoints.

Next Hop Resolution Protocol (NHRP) associates tunnel addresses with underlay endpoints. A correct path to the real hub cannot fix a mapping pointing elsewhere. Dynamic Multipoint VPN (DMVPN) combines tunneling, resolution and protected connectivity.
A tunnel interface shown as up does not establish NHRP registration, protected bidirectional traffic, routing or application delivery. Check each dependency.
labs.baseline:
Hub tunnel IP: 10.250.0.1
Hub NBMA IP: 192.0.2.10
Spoke tunnel IP: 10.250.0.2
Approved protected overlay required; security parameters omitted
labs.observed:
interface Tunnel0
 ip nhrp map 10.250.0.1 192.0.2.99
 ip nhrp nhs 10.250.0.1
! Partial excerpt only; not a deployable tunnel configuration

evidence.title: Check the approved hub transport endpoint
evidence.output:
Approved hub underlay IP: reachable from supplied transport test.
Configured 192.0.2.99: no response.
evidence.meaning: Transport to the intended hub exists; do not equate that with overlay service.

evidence.title: Compare tunnel mapping with inventory
evidence.output:
Supplied mapping summary:
10.250.0.1 -> NBMA 192.0.2.99
Approved inventory: 10.250.0.1 -> 192.0.2.10
evidence.meaning: The mapping points at a different underlay address from the approved hub.

evidence.title: Inspect the hub session
evidence.output:
Supplied session summary: hub peer not UP
No receiving-user traffic acceptance recorded.
evidence.meaning: There is no evidence of a functioning protected overlay session or staff exchange.

decisions.question: Which mismatch should be resolved first?

options.label: The hub tunnel address maps to the wrong NBMA endpoint.
options.feedback: The supplied mapping and inventory disagree while the real hub is reachable through the underlay.

options.label: Every protected tunnel needs encryption removed for testing.
options.feedback: Removing protection changes the service and is unnecessary to identify this mapping mismatch.

options.label: A successful underlay ping proves DMVPN is restored.
options.feedback: The overlay session and receiving-user task are still unverified.

decisions.question: What belongs in the bounded change plan?

options.label: Invent a new crypto profile and rotate keys.
options.feedback: No evidence supports a security-profile change; this exercise supplies no keying configuration.

options.label: Send user traffic over an unprotected bypass.
options.feedback: That does not restore the required protected service.

options.label: Correct the approved tunnel-to-NBMA mapping on the authorized lab spoke, preserving the required protection.
options.feedback: Verify the device syntax and configuration owner, keep the previous value for rollback, then check registration and protected traffic.

decisions.question: Which checks establish the required service?

options.label: Tunnel0 says up/up.
options.feedback: An interface status alone does not establish the overlay dependencies.

options.label: Correct mapping, hub session UP, expected routes, protected counters increasing both ways and a new report received.
options.feedback: These are distinct acceptance observations; counters are lab-provided evidence, not instructions to configure a cryptographic device.

options.label: The hub underlay ping succeeds.
options.feedback: It succeeded before correction and never proved overlay acceptance.

labs.recovery:
Mapping: 10.250.0.1 -> 192.0.2.10
Hub session: UP; expected service route installed
Supplied protected-flow counters: transmit and receive increase
New report R-108 received through the required protected path.
labs.impact: Leader brief: transport to the hub was available, but the spoke referenced the wrong endpoint for its overlay. Protected service and the tested report exchange were verified after the mapping correction.
labs.practical: In a permitted isolated vendor lab, label inner and outer addresses on a packet diagram. Compare the mapping and session tables. An instructor supplies security status; do not substitute this page for device security or COMSEC procedures.

labs.title: Windows identity: trace clock skew before resetting accounts
labs.bridge: Supports identity-dependent applications on server infrastructure; not a BCCS/TSI domain design.
labs.objective: Correlate an explicit authentication error with time-source evidence without weakening authentication.
labs.scenario: The training client resolves the server and reaches its TCP service. Domain sign-in to the fictional report service fails.
concepts: TCP reachability, authentication and authorization are different checks. Opening a port cannot prove a ticket is usable.
Kerberos tickets are time-bounded. Compare client, server and domain time evidence rather than guessing from a login failure alone.
A configured time source is not proof of recent successful synchronization. Check source, last synchronization and measured offset. Do not relax policy to hide drift.
labs.baseline:
Domain-joined client
Approved time source: domain hierarchy
Lab client/server clock acceptance: within documented domain policy
DNS and TCP service checks required separately
labs.observed:
Client is using Local CMOS Clock.
Client clock is 12 minutes ahead of lab domain controller.
Server clock agrees with domain controller.

evidence.title: Read the authentication error
evidence.output:
Service authentication failed: KRB_AP_ERR_SKEW
Client ahead of domain/server time by 00:12:00
evidence.meaning: The explicit error and comparison support a time-related authentication failure; other errors need different investigation.

evidence.title: Inspect synchronization status
evidence.output:
Source: Local CMOS Clock
Last Successful Sync Time: no recent domain synchronization in supplied record
evidence.meaning: This is inconsistent with the documented domain time dependency.

evidence.title: Separate name and TCP dependencies
evidence.output:
Name resolves to 10.20.40.20
TcpTestSucceeded: True
Authentication still fails.
evidence.meaning: The selected network path is usable, but identity remains a separate failure.

decisions.question: What is the supported diagnosis?

options.label: The user definitely lacks the application role.
options.feedback: Authorization has not yet been reached; the supplied error concerns clock skew.

options.label: DNS must be replaced because sign-in failed.
options.feedback: The named endpoint resolved and its TCP service was reached.

options.label: The client lost its approved time synchronization and its clock skew breaks authentication.
options.feedback: The error, offset and source evidence agree. This is more specific than a generic login failure.

decisions.question: Which correction preserves the intended identity design?

options.label: Disable time checks or extend ticket tolerance until login works.
options.feedback: That hides the synchronization fault and changes authentication policy.

options.label: Restore authorized domain time synchronization, verify offset and retry normal authentication.
options.feedback: Use the administrator-approved procedure; retain logs and avoid unnecessary account or domain changes.

options.label: Repeatedly reset the user password.
options.feedback: Password changes do not correct the observed clock offset.

decisions.question: What evidence should the recovery handoff contain?

options.label: Approved time source and recent sync, acceptable measured offset, successful normal sign-in and a new report received.
options.feedback: This connects the clock correction to authenticated application use; it does not infer every account or server is healthy.

options.label: The displayed desktop clock looks close.
options.feedback: Visual similarity does not establish synchronization source, offset or authentication.

options.label: A TCP connection still succeeds.
options.feedback: TCP already succeeded while authentication failed.

labs.recovery:
Source: lab domain hierarchy
Recent synchronization: recorded; measured offset: 0.2 seconds
Normal authentication and assigned-role check: success
Report R-109 received by intended user.
labs.impact: Leader brief: the tested client had working name and TCP access but failed identity checks because of clock drift. Normal authenticated report delivery was verified after time synchronization was restored.
labs.practical: On an isolated domain lab or supplied log set, identify time source, synchronization age and offset. Trace an authentication event to its client, server and domain context. Explain why a password reset is not a clock repair.

labs.title: Linux services: diagnose a full filesystem
labs.platform: Linux VM / systemd / GNU-style df concepts
labs.bridge: Server administration skills for infrastructure supporting mission applications; service and disk layout are fictional.
labs.objective: Distinguish a powered VM, a running service, free bytes, free inodes and application progress.
labs.scenario: The VM is running, but the report queue stops accepting updates. The data directory is on the /var filesystem.
concepts: VM power and guest OS availability do not establish application health. A service can fail when its data filesystem cannot accept writes.
Filesystems can exhaust bytes or inodes. df -h examines byte capacity; df -i examines inode capacity. Check the actual data path, not an unrelated mount.
Service status says whether a unit is active; the journal explains failures. Restarting without resolving the write failure usually reproduces the outage.
labs.baseline:
Data path: /var/lib/training-feed
Mount: /dev/vdb1 on /var
Service: training-feed.service
Approved capacity alert: before the data mount is full
labs.observed:
[Service]
ExecStart=/opt/training-feed/bin/feed
WorkingDirectory=/var/lib/training-feed
# Fictional application; no BCCS/TSI service names inferred

evidence.title: Inspect the data filesystem
evidence.output:
Filesystem /dev/vdb1
Size 20G; Used 20G; Avail 0; Use% 100%; Mounted on /var
evidence.meaning: The filesystem containing the application data has no available byte capacity in this supplied case.

evidence.title: Check inode capacity independently
evidence.output:
Filesystem /dev/vdb1
IUse% 12%; IFree 1150000; Mounted on /var
evidence.meaning: Inodes remain available. The evidence supports exhausted byte capacity rather than inode exhaustion.

evidence.title: Correlate status and unit logs
evidence.output:
Companion systemctl status: failed
Fictional feed log: write /var/lib/training-feed/queue.db failed: No space left on device
Service exited with failure.
evidence.meaning: The application write failure occurs on the same full filesystem. These are invented teaching messages, not an Army application transcript.

decisions.question: Which failure is supported?

options.label: The hypervisor must be powered off.
options.feedback: The running guest supplied filesystem and service observations.

options.label: Exhausted byte capacity on /var prevents the service from writing its queue.
options.feedback: The path, byte-capacity result and write error agree; inode availability rules out a competing explanation.

options.label: A new default gateway is required.
options.feedback: Changing routing does not free space on the local data filesystem.

decisions.question: Which recovery plan protects the data?

options.label: Identify growth and apply approved retention, archival or capacity expansion; validate available space before controlled service recovery.
options.feedback: Check backups and ownership. Preserve the database and evidence; use the documented storage procedure and rollback plan.

options.label: Delete the queue database and every log file.
options.feedback: Unreviewed deletion can destroy reports and diagnostic evidence.

options.label: Restart the service repeatedly until it works.
options.feedback: The full data filesystem remains unchanged; restarts alone do not create capacity.

decisions.question: What confirms the service recovered?

options.label: The VM remains powered on.
options.feedback: The VM was already on during the failure.

options.label: The service process starts once.
options.feedback: That does not demonstrate sustained writes, queue progress or delivery.

options.label: Verify byte/inode headroom, stable unit status, no recurring write errors, queue progress and a new report received.
options.feedback: This tests the repaired dependency and the downstream user task; monitor growth to detect recurrence.

labs.recovery:
/var: 65% bytes used; 12% inodes used
training-feed.service: active (running)
No recurring write errors during the lab observation window
Queue advances; report R-110 received.
labs.impact: Leader brief: the guest stayed online, but its full data filesystem stopped report processing. Capacity and stable queue progress were verified after the approved storage recovery; monitor growth and report any remaining backlog.
labs.practical: In a disposable VM with a dedicated small test volume, inspect df -h, df -i, systemctl status and journalctl. Use instructor-provided sample data, never fill the root disk or delete a real application database. Document the data-preserving recovery.

labs.title: VM networking: local health is not remote service
labs.bridge: Applies to services on VM infrastructure; does not prescribe BCCS/TSI virtual switches or application bindings.
labs.objective: Trace guest listener scope before blaming the hypervisor, switch or firewall.
labs.scenario: A fictional application is healthy from inside its VM, but remote clients cannot connect. The approved service design calls for the guest service IP, not loopback.
concepts: A connected virtual NIC does not prove the guest process is listening on an address reachable through that NIC.
127.0.0.1 is loopback. A process bound only there accepts local connections but not connections to the guest service IP.
Check IP/route, socket address and port, permitted policy and application response separately. Exposing a listener requires the approved interface and access controls.
labs.baseline:
Guest IP: 10.20.40.20/24
Fictional lab HTTP service: TCP 8080
Approved bind address: 10.20.40.20
Allowed source: training client subnet only
labs.observed:
# Fictional application configuration
BIND_ADDRESS=127.0.0.1
PORT=8080
# vNIC connected; guest IP and route match baseline

evidence.title: Read the listening socket
evidence.output:
State LISTEN
Local Address:Port 127.0.0.1:8080
No listener on 10.20.40.20:8080
evidence.meaning: The process listens only on loopback. -l selects listeners, -n keeps numeric addresses, and -t selects TCP.

evidence.title: Compare local health with remote access
evidence.output:
Inside VM, http://127.0.0.1:8080/health returns 200.
Guest application process is running.
evidence.meaning: A healthy loopback response does not demonstrate exposure on the service interface. HTTP is confined to this fictional isolated lab.

evidence.title: Inspect the remote port test and policy
evidence.output:
TcpTestSucceeded: False
Supplied routing, vNIC placement and intended source policy: match baseline
No supplied evidence of a listener on the guest service IP.
evidence.meaning: A remote TCP failure alone could have many causes. The socket evidence and baseline mismatch provide the specific finding.

decisions.question: What explains local success and remote failure here?

options.label: The application is bound only to loopback instead of the approved guest IP.
options.feedback: The listener table directly confirms the mismatch, while local health explains why an inside-VM test can pass.

options.label: Every VM must have two virtual NICs.
options.feedback: No supplied design or evidence requires a second interface.

options.label: An HTTP 200 on loopback proves remote readiness.
options.feedback: That result only tests the local listener and health endpoint.

decisions.question: What correction fits the documented design?

options.label: Bind to every interface and remove all access controls.
options.feedback: Broad exposure and policy removal exceed the approved service scope.

options.label: Rebuild the entire VM.
options.feedback: The observed binding mismatch is a narrower, reversible configuration issue.

options.label: Set the approved service IP in the application configuration and perform its documented controlled reload or restart.
options.feedback: Check interface availability, change ownership and rollback. Preserve the intended client restrictions; do not assume every application reloads the same way.

decisions.question: Which result set establishes remote recovery?

options.label: The VM console opens.
options.feedback: Console access does not traverse the application listener.

options.label: The socket listens on 10.20.40.20:8080, permitted remote TCP and application tests pass, and the receiver confirms a new report.
options.feedback: This verifies exposure, policy scope and user acceptance. Production TLS and identity requirements would be checked in their own documented design.

options.label: The local health response remains 200.
options.feedback: That result was already successful during the outage.

labs.recovery:
LISTEN 10.20.40.20:8080
Permitted remote TCP test: True
Remote application exchange: success; intended access restrictions retained
Report R-111 acknowledged by receiving user.
labs.impact: Leader brief: the VM and process were running, but the service was available only inside the guest. Correcting the approved bind address restored the tested remote report exchange without expanding the intended access scope.
labs.practical: Use a disposable isolated VM and generic test application. Compare a loopback listener with a listener on its assigned guest IP. Read ss output, then test from a second permitted host. Keep the lab off operational networks.

labs.platform: TACLANE/inline IP encryption concepts — synthetic observations
labs.bridge: Foundation for protected network paths supporting C2. No security configuration, keying operation or model-specific status interpretation is supplied.
concepts: TACLANE names a family of network encryptors. Confirm the exact model, software and approved network design before applying any equipment-specific procedure. This lesson models an inline protected IP path; other product modes are outside its scope.

In this teaching model, the plaintext (PT/red) side faces the protected user network; the ciphertext (CT/black) side carries encrypted traffic across transport to the remote encryptor. Encryption and routing solve different dependencies. Color terms describe the boundary, not a license to move data between networks.

Trace both directions: source LAN, local plaintext path, protected encryptor pair and ciphertext transport, remote plaintext path, then receiving application. A link indication, reachable endpoint or healthy-looking device alone cannot establish that whole exchange.
labs.title: TACLANE: separate ciphertext transport from protected service
labs.objective: Identify plaintext and ciphertext dependencies and isolate a supplied transport fault without changing cryptographic state.
labs.scenario: The fictional staff cannot send reports across a protected path. Local client access works, but the ciphertext-side transport handoff is down. These are independent instructor observations, not actual TACLANE display text.
labs.baseline:
Source PT LAN -> local encryptor
CT transport -> remote encryptor -> receiver PT LAN
Approved CT handoff: connected to the designated transport port
Approved receiving-user task: new report accepted
No security parameters or key material are shown.
labs.observed:
Local plaintext client path: available
Ciphertext transport handoff: physical link down
No ciphertext forwarding beyond that handoff
Peer/protected user exchange: not yet verified

evidence.title: Check the local plaintext boundary
evidence.command: Instructor-supplied fictional observation; no TACLANE command or menu is represented
evidence.output:
Training client reaches its approved local service gateway.
No local client addressing mismatch is supplied.
evidence.meaning: This narrows the initial fault location but does not establish remote protected service.

evidence.title: Inspect the ciphertext transport handoff
evidence.command: Instructor-supplied fictional observation; no TACLANE command or menu is represented
evidence.output:
Fictional port inspection: CT handoff disconnected at the designated transport switch.
Transport port has no physical link.
The approved diagram identifies that exact handoff.
evidence.meaning: A documented physical transport break is present. This evidence does not diagnose key state or establish the health of the remote device.

evidence.title: Check remote acceptance evidence
evidence.command: Instructor-supplied fictional observation; no TACLANE command or menu is represented
evidence.output:
The new test report has not been received.
Protected-path acceptance evidence is absent.
No supplied cryptographic alarm or key-state diagnosis.
evidence.meaning: The remote staff task is unavailable. Do not infer a key fault from a failed application exchange alone.

decisions.question: Which finding is supported before changing the encryptor?

options.label: The key material must be replaced.
options.feedback: No supplied evidence identifies a key problem. The transport handoff is visibly disconnected.

options.label: The documented ciphertext transport handoff is physically disconnected.
options.feedback: The diagram and port observation locate an upstream dependency failure. Cryptographic or application health cannot yet be concluded.

options.label: The local gateway response proves the protected path is usable.
options.feedback: That only verifies the selected local path; the remote receiving task still fails.

decisions.question: What is the bounded recovery action?

options.label: Have the authorized operator restore the designated transport handoff and verify it against the approved diagram.
options.feedback: Correct the observed physical dependency and preserve the red/black boundary. Use the exact equipment publications for any further device operation.

options.label: Connect the plaintext LAN directly to the ciphertext transport.
options.feedback: That bypasses the required protection boundary and does not restore the approved service.

options.label: Change security settings until the report goes through.
options.feedback: Trial-and-error security changes are unsupported by the supplied evidence and may add failures.

decisions.question: What supports the restored-service claim?

options.label: The transport link light returns.
options.feedback: That removes one fault, but does not establish protected traffic or receiving-user acceptance.

options.label: A local client still reaches its gateway.
options.feedback: This observation was already true during the outage.

options.label: Verify transport, the authorized peer/security status, both traffic directions and a fresh report acknowledged at the receiving endpoint.
options.feedback: These are separate acceptance observations. Use model-specific authorized status guidance rather than guessing from generic labels.

labs.recovery:
Reference observations after the approved handoff repair:
CT transport forwarding restored
Authorized operator confirms the required protected peer state
Bidirectional protected test traffic confirmed
New report T-201 received and acknowledged
labs.impact: Leader brief: the tested protected reporting path was unavailable because its ciphertext transport handoff was disconnected. Restoring the handoff and verifying the protected exchange recovered that report task; other peers and services are not covered.
labs.practical: With an instructor, label PT/red and CT/black on an approved training diagram and trace both directions. Compare supplied link, transport, peer and receiving-user evidence. For any actual device, obtain the model/software operator manual and authorized instruction; do not infer menus, alarms, keying or security actions from this workbench.

labs.platform: TACLANE/inline IP encryption concepts — synthetic observations
labs.bridge: Foundation for protected network paths supporting C2. No security configuration, keying operation or model-specific status interpretation is supplied.
concepts: TACLANE names a family of network encryptors. Confirm the exact model, software and approved network design before applying any equipment-specific procedure. This lesson models an inline protected IP path; other product modes are outside its scope.

In this teaching model, the plaintext (PT/red) side faces the protected user network; the ciphertext (CT/black) side carries encrypted traffic across transport to the remote encryptor. Encryption and routing solve different dependencies. Color terms describe the boundary, not a license to move data between networks.

Trace both directions: source LAN, local plaintext path, protected encryptor pair and ciphertext transport, remote plaintext path, then receiving application. A link indication, reachable endpoint or healthy-looking device alone cannot establish that whole exchange.
labs.title: TACLANE: healthy protected path, missing plaintext return route
labs.objective: Distinguish a protected-path observation from downstream routing and prove both directions of the supported exchange.
labs.scenario: The fictional encryptor pair passes a separate authorized protected-path test. A client request reaches the server, but the reply never returns. The supplied remote plaintext router has no route to the client subnet.
labs.baseline:
Client LAN: 10.31.10.0/24 (provided, no subnet calculation needed)
Server LAN: 10.42.20.0/24
Remote PT router must use the approved next hop for the client LAN
No unprotected bypass is permitted
labs.observed:
Authorized protected-path test: passes independently
Server receives client request and generates response
Remote PT router: no matching client-LAN route or default
No approved path for the reply in the supplied table

evidence.title: Separate the protected-path test
evidence.command: Instructor-supplied fictional observation; no TACLANE command or menu is represented
evidence.output:
Authorized operator reports the separate peer/protected-path test meets its documented criteria.
These criteria are not device menu or alarm definitions.
evidence.meaning: This evidence supports that bounded test, not every attached network or application.

evidence.title: Inspect the remote plaintext route
evidence.command: Instructor-supplied fictional observation; no TACLANE command or menu is represented
evidence.output:
Destination client LAN: 10.31.10.0/24
Remote PT router lookup: no matching route; no default
Instructor trace: reply dropped at that router
evidence.meaning: The return-path lookup identifies a routing dependency outside the tested protected exchange.

evidence.title: Compare application and traffic evidence
evidence.command: Instructor-supplied fictional observation; no TACLANE command or menu is represented
evidence.output:
Server receives new client request T-202.
Server generates its reply.
Client does not receive the reply.
evidence.meaning: One-way application flow is consistent with the supplied return-route failure. More than a protected peer indication is needed for user acceptance.

decisions.question: Which fault explains the observed one-way exchange?

options.label: The remote plaintext router lacks the approved return route to the client LAN.
options.feedback: The router lookup and reply trace identify that dependency even though the separate protected-path test passes.

options.label: Every healthy peer indication proves all application routes are correct.
options.feedback: A protected-path test does not populate downstream routing or prove application acceptance.

options.label: The encryptor must be replaced because one application fails.
options.feedback: The supplied evidence locates a narrower return-routing fault; replacement is unsupported.

decisions.question: Which correction preserves the approved design?

options.label: Remove protection and bridge the two LANs.
options.feedback: That changes the required security boundary rather than fixing the documented return path.

options.label: Change the provided subnet plan at both sites.
options.feedback: The supplied addresses match the plan; the missing return route is the specific finding.

options.label: Restore the approved client-LAN route on the responsible plaintext router through its authorized change process.
options.feedback: Use the documented next hop and routing method, retain rollback information, and repeat the receiving-user exchange. No route value is invented here.

decisions.question: What does recovery require?

options.label: Repeat only the already-passing protected-path test.
options.feedback: It passed before the routing correction and did not establish application recovery.

options.label: Confirm the return route and forwarding, repeat the protected-path acceptance check, and verify the client receives the new server response.
options.feedback: The route and two-way user transaction test the repaired dependency and required service together.

options.label: Show that the server received a request once.
options.feedback: The server already received requests while the reply path failed.

labs.recovery:
Reference observations after the approved return-route repair:
Client LAN route selected via documented PT next hop
Reply forwards toward the required protected path
Protected-path acceptance remains satisfied
Client receives the response to new test T-203
labs.impact: Leader brief: the separate protected-path test passed, but a missing remote plaintext return route prevented the tested client exchange. The approved route repair and a new two-way transaction verified recovery for that client/server task.
labs.practical: Use an isolated generic routed lab or instructor-supplied packet trace to follow a request and reply. Treat encryptor status as supplied evidence; do not emulate keys or cryptographic behavior. Explain why a route repair and a protected-path test answer different questions, then brief the exact supported task.
